In other words, if you have 10 stocks with this combination, the number of stocks that beat the consensus estimate could be as high as seven.
The Zacks Earnings ESP compares the Most Accurate Estimate to the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the quarter; the Most Accurate Estimate is a version of the Zacks Consensus whose definition is related to change. The idea here is that analysts revising their estimates right before an earnings release have the latest information, which could potentially be more accurate than what they and others contributing to the consensus had predicted earlier.
Lam Research has an Earnings ESP of +2.25% at the moment, suggesting that analysts have grown bullish on its near-term earnings potential. Investors should note, however, that a negative Earnings ESP reading is not indicative of an earnings miss, but a negative value does reduce the predictive power of this metric.
Many companies end up beating the consensus EPS estimate, though this is not the only reason why their shares gain. Additionally, some stocks may remain stable even if they end up missing the consensus estimate.

Texas Instruments and Lam Research Report Earnings: AI Equipment Boom Meets Analog Rebound
Lam Research and Texas Instruments both report after the close on Wednesday, and each faces a different kind of pressure: one must prove AI equipment demand is still accelerating, while the other needs to show its industrial recovery has real…
Published October 20, 2026, 7:50am ET · 3 min read
Automated robotic arms meticulously assemble electronic components on an advanced manufacturing line, illustrating the high-tech production methods driving growth in the semiconductor industry, particularly for AI equipment and industrial applications. © Shutterstock
Two chip stocks from opposite ends of the industry report on Wednesday, October 21, after the market close. Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX | LRCX Price Prediction) has to show that AI equipment demand is still accelerating. Texas Instruments (NASDAQ:TXN) has to show that its industrial and auto rebound can last.
Texas Instruments hosts its call at 3:30 p.m. Central time (4:30 p.m. ET). Lam follows at 5:00 p.m. ET.
Texas Instruments Faces a Test of Its Own Guidance
Texas Instruments makes analog chips that handle real-world signals like power and temperature. It also makes embedded processors, the small control chips built into machines. On its prior earnings call, Texas Instruments said revenue rose 13% sequentially and 23% year over year. Industrial, data center, and automotive customers led the growth.
Texas Instruments guided third-quarter revenue to $5.65 billion to $6.15 billion and EPS to $2.23 to $2.57. The consensus EPS estimate of $2.42 falls inside that range, so the fourth-quarter outlook carries more weight. Management said industrial revenue remains below its 2022 peak and customer inventories have not been rebuilt. Auto demand picked up, led by electric vehicles and hybrids in China. Shares are up 59.2% year to date.
Lam Research Rides AI Demand Into Record Guidance
Lam sells deposition and etch tools, the machines that add and carve away thin layers of material on silicon wafers. On its prior earnings call, Lam said it delivered record revenue, operating margin, and earnings per share “as AI-driven demand continues to reshape the semiconductor industry,” positioning it for “a third consecutive year of outperformance in 2026.”
Lam guided September-quarter revenue to $8.1 billion, plus or minus $400 million, and EPS to $2.15 plus or minus $0.15. It also raised its 2026 forecast for wafer fab equipment spending (what the whole industry spends on chipmaking tools) to the low $150 billion range.
In an August 26 Bloomberg Businessweek report, Lam Research said its advanced packaging business is growing more than 70% year over year. Advanced packaging stacks memory and processor chips in three dimensions and wires them together, so AI hardware works like one large system. Lam shares are down 12.1% over the past week and up 59.0% year to date.
Consensus Points to Steep Year-Over-Year Gains
Jim Cramer described the demand picture on October 19, saying CPUs are “going to be in very short supply, which I think is absolutely true because Taiwan Semi can’t make all the ones that they have.” He added, “There’s tremendous demand, and there’s also an inability to build.” On October 9, he said, “Taiwan Semi controlled pretty much any chip stock.”
When chipmakers cannot build fast enough, they add factory capacity, and that means buying more deposition and etch tools from Lam. Lam said the industry remains meaningfully undersupplied, with several new fabs expected to come online by the end of 2027. The same buildout is pulling in power, cooling, and networking suppliers alongside the chipmakers. (We rounded up seven of those names in a free AI infrastructure report.)
What Each Company Must Prove on Wednesday
Texas Instruments needs a fourth-quarter outlook showing that industrial and automotive demand is still climbing. Lam needs revenue close to its $8.1 billion guidance and more detail on 2027, a year management already called a potentially strong setup.

Lam Research recently reported record quarterly revenue of US$6.72b, 30% higher year on year, with earnings per share and forward revenue guidance both ahead of analyst expectations, supported by demand linked to AI, 5G and advanced automotive chips.
The same quarter underlined how Lam Research's tools and service contracts are tied directly to wafer capacity for AI and complex memory. This turns chipmakers' long dated fab build plans into multi quarter visibility on equipment orders.

Q2 Rundown: Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX) Vs Other Semiconductor Manufacturing Stocks
Earnings results often indicate what direction a company will take in the months ahead. With Q2 behind us, let's have a look at Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX) and its peers.
The semiconductor industry is driven by demand for advanced electronic products like smartphones, PCs, servers, and data storage. The need for technologies like artificial intelligence, 5G networks, and smart cars is also creating the next wave of growth for the industry. Keeping up with this dynamism requires new tools that can design, fabricate, and test chips at ever smaller sizes and more complex architectures, creating a dire need for semiconductor capital manufacturing equipment.
The 14 semiconductor manufacturing stocks we track reported a very strong Q2. As a group, revenues beat analysts' consensus estimates by 3.5% while next quarter's revenue guidance was 6.5% above.
Amidst this news, share prices of the companies have had a rough stretch. On average, they are down 7.5% since the latest earnings results.
Founded in 1980 by David Lam, the man who pioneered semiconductor etching technology, Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX) is one of the leading providers of wafer fabrication equipment used to make semiconductors.
Lam Research reported revenues of $6.72 billion, up 30% year on year. This print was in line with analysts' expectations, and overall, it was an exceptional quarter for the company with a beat of analysts' EPS estimates and revenue guidance for next quarter exceeding analysts' expectations.
"Lam delivered record revenue, operating margin and earnings per share in the June quarter as AI-driven demand continues to reshape the semiconductor industry," said Tim Archer, Lam Research's President and Chief Executive Officer.
Interestingly, the stock is up 4.9% since reporting and currently trades at $264.60.

For months, as energy and food prices surged amid the Iran war, bonds lost their shock-absorber status as investors jacked up estimates of how high interest rates might need to go.
Add near-chronic concern ‌about developed-world governments' finances, and bonds seemed to offer little safe-haven comfort while still struggling to rival super-charged equities.
The correlation between stocks and bond yields has now turned positive for Europe and the U.S., meaning yields are more likely to fall when stocks fall.
It had been overwhelmingly negative this year, with yields rising as stocks fell, undermining bonds' traditional role as a haven during equity selloffs.
This relationship fluctuates, but this year, the correlation of U.S. stocks and bond yields in March hit its most negative since at least the 1990s, while for European assets, it reached its most negative on record in September.
(3) MSCI Proposed Stripping Indonesia of EM Status. Turkey Put on Notice, Too
Central bankers in Indonesia and Turkey already have plenty on their plates.
Now they have an MSCI headache, too.
Indonesia's central bank meets on Wednesday, while Turkish policymakers gather on Thursday, against a backdrop of high energy prices, rising borrowing costs, AI-driven market disruption and geopolitical uncertainty.
MSCI has proposed stripping Indonesia of its emerging-market (EM) status and removing it from a suite of indexes, a move that risks triggering heavy outflows and raising pressure on policymakers to hike from 5.75% rather than hold.
MSCI has also put Turkey on notice, warning of a potential downgrade if market reforms fall short by mid-2027, another complication for policymakers expected to keep cutting rates from 37%.

A health check on the Chinese economy is due on Monday, with third-quarter GDP alongside September retail sales, industrial output and fixed-asset investment data.
The latest loan prime rate follows on Tuesday and is expected to stay put after more than a year on hold.
Strong global demand for semiconductors, clean technology and other manufactured goods has kept China's economy ticking, even as domestic demand remains patchy and higher energy costs bite.
Exports have held up despite China's delicate trade balancing act with the U.S. and E.U.
The latest trade figures showed Chinese exports surging well beyond analysts' estimates, putting the country on track for another $1 trillion trade surplus this year after crossing the threshold for the first time in 2025.
The flip side: the export boom could add to trade tensions with major partners.
(4) Brazil's Presidential Runoff Happens on October 25th. Campaigning Underway
Brazil's October 25th presidential runoff is keeping markets on edge after Flávio Bolsonaro's surprise first-round lead sent stocks up 7.7% and the real almost 4% higher.
A new Quaest poll puts Bolsonaro on 46% versus Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's 44%, a technical tie.
Investors are betting a Bolsonaro win would bring tighter fiscal policy, but much may already be priced in. His choice of economic team and signs of credible reform could fuel further gains.
A Lula comeback, meanwhile, could put that rally into reverse, with the real, longer-dated bonds and state-controlled companies among the most exposed. A more conservative Congress, though, could limit how far Lula could shift policy.

Micron vs. Lam Research: Does Buying the Tool Supplier Reduce Memory-Cycle Risk?
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 8:57 PM CDT 3 min read
Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) generated $89.68 billion of operating cash in its fiscal year ended September 3. Lam Research Corporation (NASDAQ:LRCX) generated $5.86 billion in its year ended June 28. The relevant question is what remains after investment when those collections weaken. Micron and Lam Research offer different ways to invest in memory demand within our 10 Best Semiconductor Stocks to Buy for the Next Decade. Micron sells memory; Lam supplies manufacturing tools and support. Buying the supplier changes the timing and mechanism of exposure, but it does not escape customers' investment cycles.
How Much Protection Does Micron's Cash Provide in the Next Downturn?
Owning production creates a larger commitment
Micron spent $30.71 billion on property, plant and equipment before government incentives. Lam spent $966 million on capital expenditure and intangible assets. Those investments consumed about 34% and 16% of operating cash, respectively.
Hold those investment bills fixed and reduce operating cash 50%. Micron would retain about $14.13 billion after investment; Lam would retain $1.96 billion. Relative to their respective annual revenue, those residuals equal 10.6% and 8.4%. The larger factory bill does not automatically leave Micron with the weaker current cushion because its starting cash generation is exceptionally high.
Micron's memory prices can change quickly; Lam's equipment orders can respond later and fall sharply when customers postpone capacity. Our Micron liquidity analysis examines why a strong cash balance still needs to be compared with future obligations.
The supplier has more than one source of demand
Lam also serves advanced logic manufacturing, while its support business includes service, spares, upgrades and older-generation tools. That gives it exposure beyond a single memory maker's output. It does not turn the company into a subscription business or guarantee that service collections stay flat during lower factory utilization.
Micron's technology and product mix could sustain stronger economics than older memory cycles suggest. The bear case is that competitive supply eventually catches up with demand, reducing prices while substantial investment continues.
At October 16 equity values, Micron cost about 17 times annual cash after gross capital spending, versus about 68 times for Lam. If Micron's cash after investment fell 75%, its multiple would rise to about 67 at an unchanged share price. That illustrates how much exceptional memory profitability supports the apparent discount; it does not establish that a 75% decline is likely or that equal multiples imply equal value.
Lam's flexibility also depends on capital allocation. Our Lam-Applied payout comparison shows how annual repurchases and dividends can exceed cash left after investment.
Q2 2026 hedge-fund holders rose to 184 from 154 for Micron and to 139 from 123 for Lam. AQR reduced Micron shares 16%, and Arrowstreet reduced Lam shares 7%. Micron's September 30 short interest was 2.31% of float.
Lam reduces direct exposure to memory selling prices and owned-fab spending. Micron starts with a stronger cash yield and a large current funding cushion. The choice depends on confidence in memory economics versus equipment demand; neither company's latest cash flow should be treated as a permanent floor.
While we acknowledge the risk and potential of MU and LRCX as investments, our conviction lies in the belief that some AI stocks hold greater promise for delivering higher returns and doing so within a shorter time frame. ASML vs. Lam Research: How Much Protection Does Service Revenue Really Provide?
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 1:56 PM CDT 3 min read
ASML Holding N.V. (NASDAQ:ASML) reported about €3.3 billion of installed-base management sales in its September quarter. Lam Research Corporation (NASDAQ:LRCX) reported $2.47 billion of customer-support-related revenue and other in its June quarter. The labels describe different mixtures. ASML and Lam Research both feature in our 10 Best Semiconductor Stocks to Buy for the Next Decade. Both have large businesses supporting equipment already inside chip factories. That can soften a new-equipment slowdown, but calling all of that revenue recurring would give investors too much confidence.
ASML vs. Lam Research: How Much Protection Does Service Revenue Really Provide?
ASML defines installed-base management as net service and field-option sales. Its customers need to maintain costly lithography machines, while upgrades can improve their productivity. Yet upgrades remain spending decisions; the entire category should not be treated as an annually contracted subscription.
Lam's category combines service, spares, upgrades and non-leading-edge Reliant equipment. That last component is equipment sales. The reported support share therefore cannot establish how much purely recurring service revenue Lam has.
Using rounded ASML figures, installed-base sales represented about 28% of quarterly revenue. Lam's broader category represented 36.8%.
Stress the revenue mix, not an invented subscription base
Assume new-system revenue falls 20% while each support category stays flat. ASML's total sales would decline about 14.4%; Lam's would decline 12.6%. If support revenue also falls 10%, the declines become about 17.2% and 16.3%.
Lam's reported mix produces the smaller decline in this exercise, but its equipment content makes a flat support assumption less secure. Neither company discloses enough here to calculate a directly comparable service-only cushion. Lower factory utilization can also reduce demand for spares and usage-related work.
Technology leadership still needs a sensible price
ASML benefits from advanced lithography transitions; Lam benefits from increasingly complex deposition and etch processes. Both face export restrictions and delayed customer investments. Our TSMC-ASML cash comparison explains why a strong cash quarter can also reflect payment timing rather than a permanently larger earnings base.
